n: Better to be poor and honest than to be a smooth-talking fool. Integrity outweighs wealth.
Zeal without knowledge isn’t good, and rushing ahead makes you miss the way.

f.w: he that hasteth with his feet sinneth
f.g: sinneth = misses the mark, loses the way.

n: People ruin their lives through their own foolishness—and then blame and rage against the Lord.

f.w: his heart fretteth against the LORD

n: Money attracts many friends, but the poor are deserted even by their neighbor.
A false witness will be punished, and a liar won’t get away with it.

f.w: A false witness shall not be unpunished

n: Many seek favor from a ruler, and everyone is a friend to the person who gives gifts.
The poor are shunned even by relatives, and friends keep their distance. He chases after them with pleas, but they are gone.

f.g: They are not there for him—nowhere to be found.

n: Getting wisdom is loving yourself rightly; keeping understanding leads to good.

f.g: Truly cares for his own life and well-being.

n: Repeats verse 5, but with a sharper ending: the liar will perish.
Luxury doesn’t suit a fool, and it’s even worse for a slave to rule over princes—things out of their proper order.

f.w: a servant to have rule over princes

n: Good sense makes a person patient, and it is to their credit to overlook an offense.
A king’s anger is terrifying like a lion’s roar, but his favor is refreshing like dew on grass.
A foolish son brings ruin to his father, and a quarrelsome wife is like a constant leaky roof.

f.g: A steady drip from a leaky roof during a rainstorm.

n: Houses and wealth can be inherited from parents, but a wise spouse is a gift from the Lord.

f.w: a prudent wife is from the LORD

n: Laziness brings on deep sleep, and the idle go hungry.
Keeping the commandments protects your life; carelessness about your conduct leads to death.
Being kind to the poor is like lending to the Lord himself, and he will repay. King Benjamin taught the same principle.
Discipline your child while there is still hope; don’t let them destroy themselves. Many translations read the second line, “don’t set your heart on his death.”

f.w: let not thy soul spare for his crying
f.g: Or “do not set your heart on putting him to death”—don’t let neglect lead to his ruin.

n: A hot-tempered person must pay the consequences; if you rescue him, you’ll have to do it again and again.

f.g: Bailing someone out repeatedly doesn’t change them.

n: Listen to advice and accept instruction so you will be wise in the end.

f.g: Later in life, or in the end.

n: People make many plans, but the Lord’s purpose is what prevails.

f.w: the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand

n: What people really want is loyal love; better to be poor than a liar.
Reverence for the Lord leads to life; such a person rests content and untouched by harm.

f.w: The fear of the LORD tendeth to life

n: A comic picture: the sluggard dips his hand in the dish but is too lazy to lift it back to his mouth.

f.w: hideth his hand in his bosom
f.g: Better “buries his hand in the dish”—the shared bowl of food.

n: Punish a mocker and the naive will learn a lesson; correct a discerning person and they’ll gain knowledge.

f.w: Smite a scorner, and the simple will beware

n: A child who robs his father and drives out his mother brings shame and disgrace.
Stop listening to teaching that leads you away from true knowledge.

f.w: the instruction that causeth to err

n: A corrupt witness mocks justice, and the wicked gulp down evil like food.

f.g: A “witness of belial”—a worthless, corrupt witness.

n: Penalties are prepared for mockers and beatings for fools.
